discovery: Quantum cryptography: quantum key distribution based on the uncertainty principle and on quantum entanglement

nominees.name: Charles H. Bennett
nominees.affiliation: IBM Research, Thomas J. Watson Research Center, USA

nominees.name: Artur K. Ekert
nominees.affiliation: University of Oxford, UK, and Centre for Quantum Technologies, National University of Singapore

motivation: Bennett and Brassard (BB84, 1984) showed that the no-cloning property and the uncertainty principle of quantum measurement make it possible to distribute secret keys whose security rests on the laws of physics rather than on computational assumptions. Ekert (1991) independently linked key security to entanglement and violation of Bell inequalities, which made Bell's theorem a working resource and laid the foundation for device-independent cryptography. Together these ideas created the field of quantum information technology. They led to teleportation-based quantum networks, quantum repeaters, metropolitan fibre networks, and satellite quantum communication over more than 1,000 km, now pursued worldwide. Few theoretical insights in recent physics have taken such a fundamental feature of quantum mechanics and made it into a practical, experimentally verified technology. The 2022 prize recognised the experimental foundations of entanglement. This prize would recognise the conceptual discovery that turned quantum foundations into secure communication.
